title: YOUR HEART HAS BEEN LYING TO YOU—BUT JEREMIAH 17:9 IS NOT SAYING WHAT MANY PEOPLE THINK
paragraphs: YOUR HEART HAS BEEN LYING TO YOU—BUT JEREMIAH 17:9 IS NOT SAYING WHAT MANY PEOPLE THINK

“The heart is deceitful above all things” has been quoted to silence emotions, condemn struggling believers, and prove that nobody should ever trust what they feel. But when you read Jeremiah’s actual words in their biblical context, something far more terrifying—and far more hopeful—emerges. The problem is deeper than your feelings. And the answer is greater than self-improvement.
There are lies you tell other people.
Then there are lies you tell yourself.
But perhaps the most dangerous lies are the ones you no longer recognize as lies because you have repeated them inside yourself for so long that they now sound like your own voice.
“I’m fine.”
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“It isn’t really sin.”
“God understands.”
“Everybody does it.”
“I’m only doing what makes me happy.”
“I know what the Bible says, but my situation is different.”
“I followed my heart.”
And sometimes that last sentence is spoken as though it settles everything.
Follow your heart.
Trust your heart.
Listen to your heart.
Do what feels right.

Our culture has turned the human heart into something close to an internal compass—an almost sacred voice supposedly waiting beneath everyone else’s expectations to guide us toward our authentic selves.
Then Jeremiah walks into the conversation.
And what he says is devastating.
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” — Jeremiah 17:9, KJV
But before we turn that sentence into a slogan, look closer.
The Hebrew reads:
עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וְאָנֻשׁ הוּא מִי יֵדָעֶנּוּ
ʿāqōḇ hallēḇ mikkōl, wəʾānūš hūʾ; mî yēḏāʿennū?
The word translated “heart” is לֵב (lēḇ).

In biblical Hebrew, the “heart” is not merely the place where you experience emotions. It can encompass the inner person—the realm of thinking, willing, desiring, choosing, understanding, and moral intention.
That matters enormously.
Jeremiah is not simply saying, “Your emotions are unreliable.”
He is exposing something much deeper.
Sin reaches into the control room.
It can distort what we want.
It can influence what we think.
It can reshape what we justify.
It can teach us to rename rebellion as freedom, pride as confidence, lust as love, greed as ambition, bitterness as discernment, cowardice as wisdom, and compromise as compassion.
The Hebrew word עָקֹב (ʿāqōḇ) carries the sense of being crooked, insidious, deceptive, or treacherous.
And then Jeremiah uses another startling word:
וְאָנֻשׁ (wəʾānūš).
Depending on translation and context, it has been rendered “desperately wicked,” “desperately sick,” “incurable,” or “beyond cure.”
Jeremiah is describing an inner corruption that human beings cannot simply diagnose and repair through self-confidence.
But there is something crucial that gets lost when Jeremiah 17:9 is ripped from its surroundings.
Jeremiah did not drop this verse randomly into the Bible.
Immediately before it, he contrasts two kinds of people.
“Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD.” — Jeremiah 17:5, KJV
Then comes the opposite picture:
“Blessed is the man that trusteth in the LORD, and whose hope the LORD is.” — Jeremiah 17:7, KJV
Do you see it?
The issue surrounding Jeremiah 17:9 is fundamentally an issue of trust.
Where will you place the weight of your life?
On human strength?
On yourself?
On your desires?
On what feels right today?
Or on the Lord?
Jeremiah paints the person who trusts in the LORD like a tree planted beside water, whose roots stretch toward the stream and which does not collapse when the heat comes.
Then comes the warning about the heart.
Then, immediately afterward, God says:
“I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings.” — Jeremiah 17:10, KJV
That changes the way you hear verse 9.
The heart can deceive you.
But it cannot deceive God.
You may fool your friends.
You may fool your spouse.
You may fool your church.
You may fool the people who follow you online.
You may learn Christian vocabulary so well that nobody notices what is dying behind your smile.
You can lift your hands during worship while secretly refusing to surrender the thing God has been confronting.
You can post Scripture publicly while feeding temptation privately.
You can tell everyone that you have peace when what you actually have is permission you gave yourself.
You can become so skilled at explaining your compromise that eventually even you believe the explanation.
But there is One Person in the room who has never been fooled by you.
God.
And strangely, that is not merely terrifying.
It is one of the most hopeful truths in Christianity.
Because the God who sees everything is also the God who came looking for sinners.
Imagine walking into a doctor's office carrying a disease you cannot diagnose.
You feel something is wrong, but you cannot locate it.
Then the physician discovers it.
That moment can terrify you because something hidden has finally been exposed.
But exposure is also the beginning of treatment.
Jeremiah 17:9 becomes crushing when we stop reading too early.
Because if Christianity ended with “your heart is corrupt,” Christianity would offer diagnosis without deliverance.
But the biblical story keeps moving.
God had already promised through Moses that He would deal with the human heart.
“The LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart... to love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul.” — Deuteronomy 30:6, KJV
David understood that cosmetic religion was not enough.
After the scandal of his sin with Bathsheba, after adultery, deception, abuse of power, and bloodshed had exposed what was hiding within him, David did not pray:
“God, help me follow my heart.”
He prayed:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — Psalm 51:10, KJV
Create.
Not decorate.
Not excuse.
Not affirm everything already there.
Create.
David had discovered something every sinner eventually has to discover:
We need more than behavior modification.
We need God to do something inside us that we cannot accomplish by ourselves.
And centuries later, through Ezekiel, God promised:
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you...” — Ezekiel 36:26, KJV
A new heart.
Now the story begins racing toward Jesus.
Because when Jesus arrived, He did not teach that evil was merely something outside humanity that corrupted otherwise innocent hearts.
He went straight to the source.
In Mark 7, Jesus explains that what defiles a person comes “from within, out of the heart of men,” and He names evil thoughts and sins flowing from that interior corruption.
Jesus does not flatter humanity.
But He does something infinitely better.
He saves humanity.
That distinction matters.
The Gospel does not say, “You are basically perfect; believe in yourself.”
Neither does it say, “You are hopelessly corrupt; therefore despair.”
The Gospel says that sin is more serious than you wanted to admit, grace is more astonishing than you dared to imagine, and Jesus Christ is more powerful than the heart you could never repair.
This is where Jeremiah 17:9 stops being merely a warning and begins pushing us toward our need for a Savior.
Because you cannot outsmart a heart capable of deceiving the person who owns it.
You need truth from outside yourself.
You need the Word of God.
You need the Spirit of God.
You need grace.
You need repentance.
You need Christ.
Jesus did not come merely to make dishonest hearts slightly more respectable.
He came to rescue sinners.
At the cross, the Son of God bore sin.
The One without sin stood in the place of sinners.
The One whose heart was perfectly faithful submitted Himself to the Father even when obedience led through Gethsemane toward Golgotha.
And listen to Jesus in Gethsemane.
“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.” — Luke 22:42, KJV
There is the opposite of our age's religion of self.
Our culture says, “My will be done.”
Jesus says, “Thine be done.”
Our culture says, “Follow your desires wherever they lead.”
Jesus calls people to deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow Him.
Our culture says authenticity means expressing whatever is inside you.
Jesus calls us into something infinitely greater than authenticity.
Holiness.
Freedom.
Truth.
Life.
Himself.
And this does not mean Christians should distrust every emotion forever.
That would go beyond what Jeremiah teaches.
Scripture does not teach that emotions themselves are evil. Jesus wept. Jesus had compassion. Jesus rejoiced. Jesus experienced anguish.
Nor does regeneration mean a Christian can never again misjudge desires or motives.
Believers still need Scripture, prayer, wisdom, correction, Christian community, and the sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit.
But something genuinely changes when a person belongs to Christ.
Paul writes:
Notice those words.
“In Christ.”
Christianity is not finally about learning to trust yourself more.
It is about learning to trust Christ completely.
Your identity is no longer determined by the loudest desire inside you.
Your sin does not get the final word.
Your shame does not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
Your feelings do not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Maybe that is exactly why this verse makes you uncomfortable.
Because somewhere inside your life there is something you desperately want God to approve simply because you desperately want it.
Maybe you have been asking God to bless something He has already told you to surrender.
Maybe you keep calling it “confusion” because calling it “disobedience” would require repentance.
Maybe you have been waiting for your feelings to change before obeying God.
Maybe you keep saying, “God knows my heart.”
Yes.
He does.
Jeremiah 17:10 is precisely that warning.
God knows the heart better than we do.
But for the Christian, “God knows my heart” should never merely be an excuse.
It can become an invitation.
Search me.
Expose me.
Correct me.
Cleanse me.
Lead me.
David prayed:
“Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.” — Psalm 139:23–24, KJV
That prayer is dangerous.
Because you are giving God permission to disturb the version of yourself you have worked so hard to protect.
“Search me.”
What if He exposes pride?
Search me.
What if He exposes lust?
Search me.
What if He exposes envy?
Search me.
What if He exposes bitterness you have baptized as righteous anger?
Search me.
What if He shows you that the relationship you refuse to surrender has become an idol?
Search me.
What if He exposes religious performance?
Search me.
What if the person you have been deceiving most successfully...
is you?
Search me anyway.
Because Jesus did not expose sinners in order to entertain spectators.
He called sinners to repentance and life.
Think about Peter.
Peter thought he knew his own heart.
“Though all men shall be offended because of thee, yet will I never be offended.” — Matthew 26:33, KJV
Peter was sincere.
That is what makes the story frightening.
He was not necessarily pretending.
He genuinely believed he knew what he would do.
Then came the courtyard.
Pressure.
Fear.
A question.
Another question.
Another.
And the man who was certain he would never abandon Jesus denied knowing Him three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
There are moments when life becomes your rooster.
A failure.
A secret message discovered.
An addiction exposed.
A marriage collapsing.
A friendship destroyed.
A private habit becoming public.
A night when you finally realize you have become someone you once swore you would never become.
The rooster crows.
And suddenly Jeremiah 17:9 is no longer theology on a page.
It has your fingerprints on it.
But Peter's story did not end beside that fire.
After the resurrection, Jesus came back for him.
Not because Peter's denial was insignificant.
Not because repentance was unnecessary.
Not because Jesus pretended betrayal did not matter.
Grace is not God pretending sin is harmless.
Grace is God doing for sinners what sinners could never do for themselves.
Jesus restored Peter.
The man who denied Christ became a man who publicly proclaimed Christ.
Scandal did not write Peter's final chapter.
Jesus did.
And maybe that is why you are still reading.
Because somewhere underneath everything else, you are wondering whether Jesus can rewrite yours.
After what you did.
After what was done to you.
After the secret.
After the relapse.
After the affair.
After the hypocrisy.
After the years you wasted.
After walking away.
After promising God you would never do it again—and doing it again.
Hear the Gospel carefully.
Your hope is not that your sin wasn't really that serious.
Your hope is that Jesus really is that sufficient.
Repentance does not mean hiding from Him until you become clean enough to return.
You cannot wash yourself before coming to the fountain.
Come to Christ.
Confess the sin.
Stop defending it.
Stop renaming it.
Stop blaming everybody else for it.
Bring the ugly truth into the light.
Scripture says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Those are stronger words than your shame.
The cross proves that God does not take sin lightly.
The empty tomb proves that sin and death do not have the final victory.
So when your heart tells you that you do not need repentance, answer it with Scripture.
When your heart tells you that you have sinned too badly to return, answer it with the Gospel.
When your heart says that temporary pleasure is worth eternal compromise, answer it with Christ.
When shame whispers, “Hide,” remember Adam.
When Jesus says, “Come,” remember the cross.
Do not merely follow your heart.
Bring your heart to Jesus.
Let His Word confront it.
Let His Spirit transform you.
Let His grace humble you.
Let His forgiveness free you.
And then follow Christ.
Maybe someone you love is quietly losing this battle right now.
They still smile.
Still work.
Still post.
Maybe they still attend church.
But something inside them is exhausted.
You do not need to publish private details. Simply comment, “Jesus, search my heart.”
If you are exhausted from fighting quietly, comment, “pray for me.”
If Christ has already been restoring something you thought was beyond repair, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Your honesty may become the moment another struggling believer realizes they are not the only person who needs grace.
There may come a night when your feelings become loud again and truth feels distant. Come back and remember:
The heart is not your Savior.
Jesus is.
It does not.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior earns salvation.
It cannot.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God with the resources He has entrusted to you, one biblical expression of that desire is voluntarily supporting faithful Gospel work and helping sound biblical truth reach others.
Not to prove your faith.
Not to purchase God's blessing.
Not to impress anybody.
Perhaps somebody is drowning beneath shame.
Perhaps somebody believes their scandal has already written the ending.
Perhaps they need to discover what Peter discovered beside another fire after the resurrection:
Failure may describe a chapter.
It does not have authority to write the ending when Jesus steps into the story.
Jeremiah's warning remains.
The heart is deceitful.
God searches it.
Sin is real.
Judgment is real.
But so is the cross.
So is forgiveness.
So is resurrection.
So is grace.
So is transformation.
So is Jesus.
And maybe the prayer you need tonight is not complicated at all.
“Jesus, search my heart.
Expose what I keep defending.
Forgive what I have confessed.
Break what is destroying me.
Teach me to trust Your Word above my impulses.
Create in me a clean heart.
Make my life Yours.
And when my heart lies to me...
teach me to follow You anyway.”
Because the most dangerous voice in your life may sometimes come from inside you—but the most trustworthy voice will always belong to the Shepherd who laid down His life for His sheep.
Your heart does not need to become your god.
It needs to belong to Christ.
And when Jesus takes hold of a story everyone thought was ruined, even the ugliest chapter can become evidence that grace had not finished writing.
The scandal may explain how you arrived here. Grace decides that you do not have to remain here.
